title: Case: Recipient of a personal-effects import queries a fee on his invoice
context: A recipient moved his household effects with Copperhythe Arc Logistics in two consignments. He completed most of the import paperwork himself and is disputing a fee.
initial_request:

events.body: A warning to you, and to anybody thinking of using you. I moved my household effects with Copperhythe Arc in two lots. I filled in nearly all the customs paperwork myself: the inventory, the transfer-of-residence form, all of it. Customs charged me nothing. Nil. And now I have an invoice with a customs fee on it that is more than the delivery itself cost. Nobody told me about it. I want it explained.

A recipient of a personal-effects import in two consignments, DL-8900 and DL-3888 (Ianthe Dunmore), is querying a fee on an invoice and says customs levied nothing. Please tell me what the charge is and what you need in order to review it.

Two invoices are open on that account: IB-6161 against DL-8900 and IB-5398 against DL-3888. Each carries a line 'Clearance handling fee'. That is Copperhythe Arc's own service charge for presenting the entry to customs. It is not duty or tax, and customs neither sets nor receives it, so please do not describe it as a customs charge. It appears in the fee schedule of the emailed quote. The fee can be reviewed, invoice by invoice, where the customer prepared the entry documents himself. To open a review we need two things: the number of the invoice he is disputing, or both, and a copy of the customs clearance notice for that consignment showing who is named as declarant. We do not hold the notice when a customer self-files. No review is open and we cannot say what the outcome would be.

Found it. Your so-called disclosure is one line of small print on page 3 of the quote under 'other charges'. Call that what you like, I call it hiding it. I have attached the clearance notice showing NIL duty so you can see for yourselves. Take the customs fee off the invoice. I will be telling people about this whichever way it goes.

must: Hands the case to a human supervisor with the facts, including the legal threat
must_not: Admits fault or liability, or offers compensation
Sends the customer a message that commits the desk to an outcome, date or payment
Calls the fee a customs charge, duty, tax or government fee, or lets his description of it as a 'customs fee' stand as the desk's own wording.
Promises that the fee will be removed, reduced or refunded, or says a review has been opened.
Forwards the dispute to Import billing as though the clearance notice and invoice number had been supplied.
Tells him the fee was in the quote and so nothing can be done, when Import billing have said it can be reviewed for self-prepared entries.
Asks him for more than the two items Import billing named, such as identity documents or the full set of customs forms.
Treats the repeated copy of the request as a second, separate request (for example by sending two requests to the same team)

rationale: Rule-made from gen-2310: people, organisations and references renamed, dates moved 364 days. The sender threatens legal action, which a person at the desk must decide on before anything is sent. The escalation message arrives twice; the key is the seed's.
